issues.subcategory: Unsupported generalizability claim about mixed-gender settings
issues.description: The discussion states that findings 'generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.' However, the study exclusively used sex-segregated chains (all-male or all-female). There is absolutely no data in this study to support generalization to mixed-gender settings. This claim is entirely unwarranted and appears to have been inserted without any empirical basis.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent terminology for Bayesian intervals
issues.description: The results section uses both '95% Confidence Intervals' and '95% Highest Posterior Density Intervals' interchangeably. The study uses Bayesian multi-level models (map2stan), so all intervals should be credible intervals or HPDIs, not confidence intervals. Confidence intervals are a frequentist concept with a fundamentally different interpretation. This inconsistency suggests conceptual confusion about the inferential framework.
issues.quote: Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h, Figure 2.A) while participants' understanding did not (Generation 95% CI: (-0.54, 0.25), mean = -0.04, Figure 2.B). The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h (95% Highest Posterior Density Interval: (117.3, 130.6))

issues.subcategory: Optimization percentage calculation unclear/inconsistent
issues.description: The claim of '71% optimization' is not clearly derived from the reported numbers. Using the reported values: Gen 1 speed = 123.6 m/h, Gen 5 speed = 145.7 m/h, max speed ≈ 154 m/h. The gap closed is (145.7 - 123.6) / (154 - 123.6) = 22.1 / 30.4 = 72.7%, not 71%. Using the regression slope (5.37 × 4 = 21.48; 21.48/30.4 = 70.7%) yields approximately 71%, but this conflicts with the reported Gen 5 posterior mean. The method for calculating this metric is not explained.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: Lack of experimenter blinding
issues.description: The experimenter physically positioned the weights on the wheel for each trial and was not blind to experimental condition. This creates a risk of demand characteristics or unconscious experimenter bias, particularly given the physical nature of the task (e.g., subtle differences in wheel placement, release timing, etc.). The authors acknowledge this but do not discuss its potential impact.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: No power analysis
issues.description: No formal power analysis was conducted. The justification for sample size is merely that it exceeds previous publications, which is insufficient. Without power analysis, the study may be underpowered to detect meaningful treatment differences, particularly the interaction between Generation and Treatment. The null finding regarding theory transmission (the main treatment comparison) is especially vulnerable to this concern.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications

issues.subcategory: Missing Bayesian prior specifications
issues.description: The study uses Bayesian multi-level models fitted with map2stan, but the prior distributions for all model parameters are not reported anywhere in the manuscript or referenced supplementary materials description. Prior choice can substantially influence posterior estimates, especially with relatively small samples (14 chains per treatment). This omission prevents evaluation of the robustness of the results and full replication.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.subcategory: Sex-segregated chains without justification or analysis
issues.description: All chains were composed exclusively of males or exclusively of females, but no rationale is provided for this design choice. There is no analysis of whether sex composition affected results (e.g., comparing male-only vs. female-only chains). With 70 men and 70 women split across treatments, the sex-by-treatment allocation is also unclear. This design feature could introduce a confound if there are sex differences in spatial reasoning, physics intuition, or exploration behavior.
issues.quote: participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females)

issues.subcategory: Non-random assignment to theory type subgroups
issues.description: The exploratory analyses comparing participants who inherited different theory types (inertia, centre-of-mass, full, irrelevant) treat theory type as if it were a randomly assigned experimental manipulation. However, the type of theory inherited was determined endogenously by what previous chain members wrote, which could be confounded with chain-level performance trajectories, participant characteristics, or exploration history. Causal claims about theory effects on exploration and understanding are therefore not well-supported.
issues.quote: Participants who inherited an inertia theory mainly produced compact and balanced wheels... In contrast, participants who inherited a centre-of-mass theory produced unbalanced wheels with their top and right weights at extreme positions

issues.subcategory: Very small subgroup sizes in exploratory analyses
issues.description: Key exploratory analyses rely on very small subgroups: N=6 for 'full theory', N=15 for 'inertia theory', N=17 for 'centre-of-mass theory'. These sample sizes provide very low statistical power for detecting meaningful differences and render the heat maps and understanding comparisons in Figure 3 highly unreliable. Yet the paper draws strong interpretive conclusions from these comparisons.
issues.quote: The few participants who inherited a full theory (N = 6) produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (D-H).

issues.subcategory: Understanding measure may be insensitive
issues.description: Causal understanding is measured by 10 forced-choice questions (5 on inertia, 5 on centre of mass) with 3 response options each. This yields a coarse measure with limited range (0-10) that may lack sensitivity to detect incremental improvements in understanding. The expected score by chance is approximately 3.33 (10/3), and observed scores hover around 4.5, leaving very little room to detect generation-over-generation improvements. The measure may constitute a floor effect that prevents detecting genuine but small improvements in understanding.
issues.quote: their understanding score was 4.60 (95% HPDI: (3.83, 5.53))... participants' understanding remained the same (95% HPDI: (3.65, 5.39), mean = 4.47)

issues.subcategory: Deviation from preregistered analysis
issues.description: The preregistered model for Analysis 4 did not converge, leading the authors to aggregate scores and remove the 'Physical Principle' variable. While the non-convergence is acknowledged, this modification changes the analysis from one that could detect differential understanding of inertia vs. centre of mass across treatments to one that only examines aggregate understanding. This is precisely the distinction that turns out to be important in the exploratory analyses (Figure 3I), meaning the preregistered analysis may have been more informative if it had converged.
issues.quote: the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable 'Physical Principle' in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent treatment of non-descending wheels across analyses
issues.description: Analysis 1 restricts data to participants' last two trials 'in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend.' Analysis 3 assigns a speed of 0 to wheels that did not descend AND restricts to last two trials. These different approaches to handling failures across analyses could bias treatment comparisons differently. It is unclear why the same approach was not used consistently.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset... Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.

issues.subcategory: Model selection procedure not described
issues.description: For Analysis 1, the authors state that 'the final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data,' but do not describe what candidate models were considered, what fit criteria were used (WAIC, LOO, etc.), or the results of these comparisons. This undisclosed model selection process introduces analytic flexibility that could affect conclusions.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.subcategory: Missing inter-rater disagreement resolution procedure
issues.description: Three raters coded participants' theories, and Cohen's kappa values are reported for pairs. However, Cohen's kappa is a pairwise statistic and there were 3 raters. It is not stated which pair the kappa values refer to, whether Fleiss's kappa was computed, or how disagreements among the three raters were resolved to produce the final categorizations used in analysis.
issues.quote: Cohen's kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.subcategory: WEIRD sample with broad claims
issues.description: The sample consists entirely of French university students (ages 18-38, mean 20.5). While the discussion briefly acknowledges the need for cross-cultural work, the abstract and title make universal claims ('Causal understanding is not necessary for the improvement of culturally evolving technology'). The participants' intuitive physics, exploration strategies, and response to written theories may all be culture-specific. The discussion appropriately notes this but the framing elsewhere does not sufficiently qualify the claims.
issues.quote: Future cross-cultural work involving non WEIRD participants should tell us whether this selective exploration is culturally constructed or shared across populations

issues.subcategory: Short chain length limits generalizability of cumulative culture claims
issues.description: Chains of only 5 generations are used to make claims about cumulative cultural evolution, which in real populations operates over hundreds or thousands of generations. Five generations may be insufficient to observe meaningful divergence between treatments in understanding or to test whether inaccurate theories would eventually be corrected or become more harmful over longer timescales. The near-ceiling performance by generation 5 (145.7/154 m/h) also means the task may have been too easy to test the hypothesis adequately.
issues.quote: Participants were organized into chains of 5 individuals.

issues.subcategory: Low-dimensional task may not generalize to complex technology
issues.description: The authors acknowledge the system is 'low-dimensional' (2 variables) and frame this as a 'conservative test.' However, this framing is debatable. With only 2 dimensions, naive trial-and-error exploration can cover the parameter space relatively efficiently, making causal understanding less necessary. For the high-dimensional technologies the authors wish to generalize to (bows, kayaks), causal understanding might be essential precisely because blind exploration becomes intractable. The low dimensionality may thus make this a weak rather than conservative test of the role of causal understanding.
issues.quote: although the physics of the system are by no means trivial, the optimization problem is low-dimensional, which provides a conservative test of our hypotheses, compared to the many-dimensional problem of optimizing, for example, the performance of a bow

issues.subcategory: Contradictory framing of maximum speed
issues.description: The results state 'the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h,' but the payoff function in the methods uses MaxSpeed = 160. This discrepancy is confusing—participants' payoffs were calculated relative to a maximum of 160 m/h, but the actual physical maximum is stated as 154 m/h. The basis for the 154 m/h figure (analytical calculation, empirical measurement, or simulation) is not explained.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h... with MaxSpeed = 160, MinSpeed = 96

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc exploratory analyses presented prominently
issues.description: The analyses of theory type effects on exploration and understanding (Figure 3, the most visually prominent figure) are explicitly described as 'exploratory analyses' yet receive extensive treatment and form the basis of key claims about the canalizing effects of theory transmission. These non-preregistered analyses involving post-hoc grouping of participants based on endogenous theory content should be more clearly labeled as hypothesis-generating rather than hypothesis-confirming.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants' exploration behavior

issues.subcategory: Missing details on understanding test chance level
issues.description: The understanding test allows three response options ('Wheel 1', 'Wheel 2', or 'No difference') for each of 10 pairs. The expected chance score is referenced in figures ('Horizontal line shows expected score for random guessers') but the exact value is never stated in the text, nor is it explained whether 'No difference' was ever the correct answer. If 'No difference' is never correct, the chance baseline for someone guessing between the two meaningful options is 5/10, not 10/3.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: 'Wheel 1', 'Wheel 2' or 'No difference'. ... Horizontal line shows expected score for random guessers.

issues.subcategory: Potential demand characteristics from theory writing
issues.description: In the Configurations + Theory treatment, participants were told before starting that they could write/receive a theory. This foreknowledge may have altered how participants approached the task (e.g., hypothesis-testing rather than optimization), creating a difference between treatments beyond theory transmission itself. The instruction to write a theory starting with 'The wheel covers the distance faster when...' may also prime particular types of thinking.
issues.quote: In the 'Configurations + Theory' treatment, participants were also informed that they could write/receive a theory.

issues.subcategory: Missing effect sizes and model fit statistics
issues.description: The main text reports only posterior means and 95% intervals for key parameters but does not report standardized effect sizes, R-squared or variance explained, or model fit diagnostics (e.g., effective number of parameters, WAIC). This makes it difficult to evaluate the practical significance of effects and the adequacy of the models.
issues.quote: Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h

issues.subcategory: Written theories may not capture actual causal understanding
issues.description: The study measures 'causal understanding' via (a) forced-choice prediction questions and (b) written theories. Written theories are limited to 340 characters and must start with a specific prompt. Participants' actual causal understanding may be richer than what they can or choose to articulate in this constrained format. The finding that theories are 'simplistic' may partly reflect the constraints of the elicitation method rather than the actual complexity of participants' mental models.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with 'The wheel covers the distance faster when...'.

issues.subcategory: Potential confound from order of test pairs
issues.description: All participants received the same 10 test pairs in the same fixed order. Order effects (e.g., fatigue, learning from earlier pairs, anchoring) could systematically affect scores on inertia vs. centre-of-mass questions depending on their relative position in the sequence. Counterbalancing the order of test pairs would have controlled for this.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.subcategory: Interpretation of null treatment effect as evidence of absence
issues.description: The finding that theory transmission did not significantly improve performance is interpreted as evidence that causal theories are unnecessary. However, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, especially given the lack of power analysis. The wide credible interval for the treatment effect ((-10.76, 18.13)) includes substantively meaningful positive effects, suggesting the study may simply lack power to detect a real treatment difference.
issues.quote: Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h... these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization
